question.text: "Occult" posttraumatic lesions of the knee: can magnetic resonance substitute for diagnostic arthroscopy?
question.context: We investigated the actual role of MRI versus arthroscopy in the detection and characterization of occult bone and/or cartilage injuries in patients with previous musculoskeletal trauma of the knee, pain and severe functional impairment. Occult post-traumatic osteochondral injuries of the knee are trauma-related bone and/or cartilage damage missed at plain radiography. We retrospectively selected 70 patients (men:women = 7:3; age range: 35 +/- 7 years) with a history of acute musculoskeletal trauma, negative conventional radiographs, pain and limited joint movements. All patients were submitted to conventional radiography, arthroscopy and MRI, the latter with 0.5 T units and T1-weighted SE. T2-weighted GE and FIR sequences with fat suppression. We identified three types of occult post-traumatic injuries by morpho-topographic and signal intensity patterns: bone bruises (no. 25), subchondral (no. 33) and osteochondral (no. 35) injuries. Arthroscopy depicted 45 osteochondral and 19 chondral injuries. A bone bruise was defined as a typical subcortical area of signal loss, with various shapes, on T1-weighted images and of increased signal intensity on T2-weighted and FIR images. The cortical bone and articular cartilage were normal in all cases, while osteochondral injuries exhibited associated bone and cartilage damage with the same abnormal MR signal intensity. Sprain was the mechanism of injury in 52 cases, bruise in 12 and stress in 6. In 52 sprains (30 in valgus), the injury site was the lateral compartment in 92.3% of cases (100% in valgus), associated with meniscal damage in 73% of cases (90% in valgus) and with ligament injury in 90.4% (100% in valgus). In 12 bruises, the injury site was the lateral compartment in 58.3% of cases, the knee cap in 25% and the medial compartment in 16.7%; meniscal damage was associated in 25% of cases and ligament damage in 8.3%. In 6 stress injuries, the injury site was localized in the medial tibial condyle in 80% of cases, while meniscal and ligament tears were absent.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that MRI can accurately detect occult post-traumatic osteochondral injuries in the knee, even when radiographs are negative. Arthroscopy is invasive and may not always reveal subtle injuries. Therefore, MRI can serve as a valuable substitute for arthroscopy in these cases.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: MRI accurately detected osteochondral injuries, while arthroscopy detected more significant injuries.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While arthroscopy is more invasive, it can provide a direct visualization of the joint and potentially identify injuries not seen on MRI. However, the study shows MRI's ability to detect subtle injuries, making it a reasonable alternative.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: MRI detected all 93 occult injuries (45 osteochondral, 19 chondral, 29 bone bruises) while arthroscopy only found 64 (45 osteochondral + 19 chondral). The study shows MRI has higher sensitivity for detecting these occult injuries.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: MRI identified 29 bone bruises that were missed by arthroscopy, demonstrating its superior ability to detect all types of occult injuries.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While arthroscopy provides direct visualization, MRI offers comparable diagnostic accuracy with higher sensitivity for occult injuries, making it a valuable adjunct in cases of negative radiographs with persistent symptoms.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that MRI, even with 0.5T and specific sequences, failed to reliably detect all occult osteochondral injuries compared to arthroscopy, which identified 45 osteochondral and 19 chondral injuries — suggesting MRI is insufficient as a standalone substitute. The high rate of missed injuries by MRI indicates it cannot reliably replace arthroscopy in this context.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Arthroscopy depicted 45 osteochondral and 19 chondral injuries, while MRI identified only 35 osteochondral injuries (and 25 bone bruises, 33 subchondral injuries) — implying MRI missed a significant number of osteochondral injuries.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: MRI's sensitivity was questioned due to its inability to detect all osteochondral injuries, and arthroscopy was superior in identifying them. Other imaging modalities like CT or ultrasound were not evaluated, so they were not considered as alternatives in this study.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Arthroscopy (the gold standard) could directly visualize injuries missed by radiography and MRI, such as early cartilage defects or ligament injuries, which MRI signal patterns may be non-specific. Plain radiography was negative, but MRI was positive; however, MRI lacks the ability to assess real-time ligament or meniscal integrity, making it incomplete as a stand-alone diagnostic tool.
